utterance: Hi there, I'm so glad you're here. I want you to know that this space is safe—whatever you share with me, it will stay private, and I’m here to listen without judgment. I’m curious—what’s on your mind today? What brings you in for this session?

I’ve been thinking a lot about that recent dental appointment—how it felt like walking back into a place where I was already scared, even though the actual treatment went okay. I didn’t expect to cry so much or feel so disconnected, like I was floating out of my body. It made me realize how deeply those medical settings, especially with doctors, still trigger old wounds from childhood and the sexual assault I went through. I’m not sure I’m ready to go back to the dentist yet, but I’m starting to wonder if I can find a way to feel safer in those spaces—without having to fight the fear. I just wanted to share that with you.

It sounds like that dental appointment brought up a lot of old emotions—feeling like you were walking back into a space that’s been scary for years, even when things were physically okay. The crying and dissociation must have felt overwhelming, and it’s not surprising that it triggered memories of the medical settings and trauma from childhood and the sexual assault. Thank you for sharing that so honestly. Would it be helpful to explore what part of that experience felt most difficult to carry, or what you noticed about how your body or mind reacted?

The part that felt most difficult was when the hygienist started scaling—my body just went rigid, like I was frozen. I could feel my breath catch, and my hands were shaking so bad I had to hold onto the armrest. I didn’t even realize I was crying until I looked down and saw my hands trembling. It wasn’t the pain—it was the feeling of being in that room again, like I was back in the hospital when I was a kid, or when the doctor touched me without permission. My husband was there the whole time, and I think that helped, but I still felt so far away from myself. I don’t know if I can trust the dental office to be safe again, not just for me, but for the way it makes me feel.

It wasn’t just the scaling—it was the way she moved her hands, like she was doing something invasive, and suddenly I felt like I was back in that hospital room when I was seven, and I didn’t even know what was happening. My body just shut down. I remember thinking, *this is not safe*, and I couldn’t move or breathe. The meds helped a little, but they didn’t stop the fear from rising in my chest. And the worst part? I had to pay the balance out of my own pocket—scrambled for cash, felt so exposed. It made me feel like I wasn’t just afraid of the dentist, I was afraid of being in a place where I have to be responsible for my own survival, like I still have to prove I’m not a burden. That part—feeling so small and unsafe in my own body—still haunts me.

The part that hit me the hardest was when she started scaling—my body just locked up, like I was frozen in place. I could feel my heart pounding, but my hands were numb, and I couldn’t speak. It wasn’t the pain—it was the way it felt like she was touching me without asking, like I was back in that hospital when I was seven, and the doctors didn’t explain anything. I remember thinking, *I don’t know what’s happening, and I don’t want to be here*. The meds helped, but they didn’t stop the fear from crawling up my spine. And paying the balance out of my own pocket—it made me feel like I had to be strong, like I had to prove I wasn’t just a scared person. It felt like I was carrying all that alone, even with my husband there. It still feels like a betrayal of trust—not just in the office, but in myself.

The doctors didn’t explain things, they just touched me, and I didn’t know what was happening. That memory plays over and over in my head during appointments now. Even though this time the cleaning went okay, my body still went rigid, like I was being touched without permission. I cried because it felt like I was reliving that moment—being small, powerless, and not knowing if I was safe. My husband was there, and he stayed calm, but I still felt so alone in my own skin. I keep thinking: *Can I ever trust a doctor again?* It’s not just about the procedure—it’s about whether I can feel safe in my own body.

Yeah, it’s the same pattern—those places where someone else makes decisions about my body, without asking. When I was little, I’d be in the hospital, and the doctors would just touch me, like it was normal, and I didn’t know how to say no. That’s still in my bones. And the sexual assault part—when the doctor did the kit without asking, and the students were watching—it wasn’t just about the physical thing; it was about being violated in a room that felt like a cage. I didn’t even know I was being touched until it was too late. That’s why I avoided dental visits for ten years. Not because I didn’t need help, but because I didn’t trust anyone to treat me with respect. Even now, when the cleaning went okay, my hands still shook, and I felt like I was being watched again. I don’t know if I can go back, but I don’t want to give up either. I keep thinking about how much pain I’ve carried in silence for so long—like I was supposed to just survive, not speak up. And now, when I finally show up, even with the meds, I still feel like I’m walking into a room where I have no say. But maybe that’s where the real work begins—not in avoiding, but in learning how to say, *“I’m here. I’m not okay with this. I need to be treated with care.”* I don’t know if I’m ready for that yet, but I’m starting to believe it’s possible. And that feels like a step.

The part that still hurts is paying the balance out of my own pocket. I felt like I had to prove I wasn’t just a scared person—like I had to show up strong, even when my body was shaking and I couldn’t breathe. My husband stayed with me, and he didn’t push, which meant a lot. But I still felt like I was carrying all of it alone. And now, hearing you say that maybe the real work is learning to say, *“I’m not okay with this,”* it feels like a light in the dark. I don’t know if I can say that out loud yet, not in a dental office, not in front of a doctor. But I do know this: I’m not going to run from it anymore. I’m going to keep showing up, even if it’s just one step at a time. And maybe, just maybe, I’ll learn to say what I need—without fear.

I still feel like I’m walking through a door that was meant to be locked. The way the dentist looked at me—calm, like it was nothing—made me want to shut down. I didn’t want to fight, didn’t want to make it worse, but I also couldn’t stay silent. And when I paid the balance myself, it felt like I was giving myself permission to stay in that room, to be seen, even when I was shaking. I didn’t know if I’d ever be able to say, *“I need this to be safe,”* but now, with you saying that, it feels like a word I can start to carry. Not loud, not perfect—but real. And that’s enough for now.

The dissociation came back right after I paid—it wasn’t just fear, it was like my body pulled away, like I was watching myself from the outside. I remember thinking, *“Is this real?”* because I felt so disconnected from what was happening. But when I looked at my husband and saw him just sitting there, not rushing, not pushing, it grounded me. I didn’t have to be strong. I just had to be present. And that small moment—me saying, *“I’m here,”* even if it felt like a whisper—was the first time I didn’t feel like I had to hide. I still don’t trust every doctor, but I’m learning to show up with my whole self. And that’s a start.

I cried during the payment part—not because I was weak, but because I finally felt like I was doing something real. Before, I’d avoid appointments, skip them, hide in my room, just waiting for the fear to pass. But this time, when I saw the receipt and the balance, I didn’t run. I just sat there, breathing, and let the tears come. It wasn’t about fixing anything. It was about letting myself feel the weight of it all—without pretending I was okay. And now, when I think about that moment, I don’t feel like I’m broken. I feel like I’m learning to carry my pain without losing myself. That’s what I didn’t know was possible.

I still flinch when a doctor makes eye contact, like I’m being scanned again. But today, when I sat with my husband and just let the tears fall, I didn’t pull away. I didn’t say anything to stop it. And that felt like a victory. Not because it was easy, but because I didn’t try to fix it or hide it. I just let it be. And in that moment, I realized—I don’t have to be strong to be safe. I just have to be here. Even if it hurts. Even if I’m shaking. That’s where I start.

I still feel the old panic when the lights go on in the exam room—like I’m being watched, like I’m not allowed to be quiet. But now, when that happens, I don’t run. I take a breath, and I say to myself, *“This is still mine. I don’t have to fix it. I don’t have to be okay. I just have to be here.”* And sometimes, when I’m alone, I still freeze. But I’m learning to notice it, instead of fighting it. That small shift—just noticing—feels like progress. Not because it’s perfect, but because it’s real. And real is enough.

The meds help a little—sometimes they make the panic less sharp—but they don’t stop the fear from coming back when I’m alone. I still feel it in my chest, like a knot, when I think about going back to the office. But now, when that happens, I don’t push away. I just sit with it. And I whisper to myself, *“You’re not broken. You’re just learning.”* That’s the part that keeps me from running. Not the calm, not the strength—but the quiet truth that I’m doing better than I was yesterday. And that’s enough.

I still get that tightness in my chest when I think about the next appointment, like my body is holding its breath. But now, when it happens, I don’t close my eyes or pull away. I just breathe into it, and I tell myself, *“This is not your fault. This is just your story.”* And for the first time, I don’t feel like I have to win the battle. I just have to show up. Even if it’s shaky. Even if it’s hard. That’s all I’m asking for. And it’s more than I ever thought I could do.

I remember how, before, I’d leave the room halfway through appointments just to escape the silence. Now, I stay. Not because I’m brave, but because I’m tired of pretending I’m okay. And when the silence hits—when the room goes still and my heart starts to race—I don’t run. I just sit. I don’t need to speak. I don’t need to fix anything. I just need to know I’m not alone in it. That’s what matters most. And that small act of staying… it feels like a step forward. Not because it’s perfect, but because it’s real.

I still freeze when the doctor starts talking, like my body remembers every time before. But now, when that happens, I don’t pull away. I just close my eyes and say, *“I’m here. I’m not going anywhere.”* And I don’t look at my husband—because I don’t want to make him feel like he has to fix it. I just let the fear live in me, quietly. And in that quiet, I start to feel like I’m not running from it. I’m just… holding space for it. That’s what I needed all along. Not strength. Not silence. Just presence. And that’s enough.

The payment issue still hangs over everything—how I can’t afford the meds, how I’ve been skipping doses because I can’t pay. It makes the fear feel heavier, like the clinic is just another place that won’t help me. But today, when I sat with my husband and cried without stopping, I didn’t feel guilty. I just felt… seen. And that small moment—just being allowed to be broken—was the first time I didn’t have to fix it. I don’t know if I’ll ever feel safe in those rooms again. But I do know I can sit with the fear now. And that’s more than I ever thought I could do.
